evidence_tier: Peer-reviewed. Schmidt & Hunter (1998) is a peer-reviewed review that assembles earlier meta-analytic estimates (it does not run a new meta-analysis for work samples; the work sample figure is taken from Hunter & Hunter 1984). Roth et al. (2005) is a peer-reviewed meta-analysis. Sackett et al. (2023) is a peer-reviewed focal article.

(2005): abstract only (verbatim abstract via Crossref); full text paywalled (Wiley returned 403). sponsor_and_incentive: Schmidt & Hunter (1998): academic authors (University of Iowa, Michigan State University); an earlier version was presented to Korean HR managers in Seoul in 1996 in a talk 'sponsored by Tong Yang Company'. Both authors were the main developers of validity generalization meta-analysis methods and long-time advocates of GMA testing, so they have an intellectual stake in the corrected-validity approach. Roth et al. (2005): academic authors; no commercial sponsor found in the abstract or outline [uncertain]. No author sells interview products tied to these findings.

date_and_recency: Schmidt & Hunter: published 1998 (March issue, Vol. 124 No. 2); summarises 85 years of research up to about 1996-1997; the work sample figure itself comes from Hunter & Hunter (1984), whose data are older still (largely pre-1980). Roth et al.: published December 2005; per the course outline, studies published both before and after 1982 were included. Neither predates nor addresses software engineering, take-home coding tests or AI tools.
key_claims: Schmidt & Hunter (1998): (a) GMA tests have the best validity-to-cost profile for all jobs (r = .51 for medium-complexity jobs). (b) Work sample tests have the highest single-predictor validity in their table (.54) but are costly and only usable with applicants who already know the job. (c) Structured interviews (.51) beat unstructured interviews (.38). (d) The best two-predictor combinations are GMA + integrity (.65), GMA + work sample (.63) and GMA + structured interview (.63); the latter two each add .12 (24%) over GMA alone. (e) Validity translates directly into utility (dollar value of output). Roth et al. (2005): (a) the classic Asher & Sciarrino (1974) review that fed the Hunter & Hunter (1984) .54 estimate had methodological problems (mixing job knowledge and situational judgement tests in as 'work samples', range-enhanced coefficients from extreme-group designs). (b) Integrating cleaned data, work sample validity is .26 observed and .33 corrected for criterion unreliability, about one third lower than .54. (c) Work samples correlate .32 (observed) with general cognitive ability. Per the course outline (secondary): older (pre-1982) studies show higher validity than newer ones, and incremental validity of work samples over GMA was .06 without range-restriction correction.

sample_and_method: Schmidt & Hunter (1998): a review compiling published meta-analytic validity estimates for 19 predictors, then computing two-predictor multiple regressions with GMA using estimated predictor intercorrelations. The criterion is overall job performance, mostly supervisory ratings, across a broad range of mainly US civilian jobs (the GMA estimate rests on over 32,000 employees in 515 jobs). The work sample row was not re-meta-analysed: it is lifted from Hunter & Hunter (1984). Their own examples are skilled trades (welders, machinists, carpenters, motor repair). Roth et al. (2005): a new meta-analysis (Hunter-Schmidt style, uncorrected correlations meta-analysed, then corrected for criterion unreliability only) of studies reporting work sample to job performance correlations for applicants or incumbents. Inclusion rules excluded paper-and-pencil job knowledge tests, situational judgement ('what would you do') items, contaminated ratings (same rater for test and job), range-enhanced coefficients and non-independent samples. Moderators coded: applicant vs incumbent, objective vs subjective criterion, military vs non-military, job complexity (five levels, 'computer trouble shooter' as medium high), publication date. Neither source isolates software engineers; any software roles are a small, unidentified part of mixed samples.
what_is_measured: Criterion validity of hiring methods for predicting overall job performance (mostly supervisor ratings). The work sample construct is defined as performing actual job tasks: Schmidt & Hunter call them 'hands-on simulations of part or all of the job'; Roth et al. (per outline) use 'a test in which the applicant performs a selected set of actual tasks that are physically and/or psychologically similar to those performed on the job', standardised and expert-scored, with high fidelity. For coding interviews this maps most closely to realistic take-home or pair-programming tasks, not to abstract algorithm puzzles, which arguably sit closer to GMA or job-knowledge measures.
ai_policy_in_interview: Not applicable (pre-AI research; no tooling policy discussed).
scope_and_status: Not applicable (academic research syntheses, not an employer's hiring rollout).
validity_evidence: Work sample tests: .54 in Schmidt & Hunter (1998), corrected for criterion unreliability only, inherited from Hunter & Hunter (1984). Roth et al. (2005) re-estimate: .26 observed, .33 corrected for criterion unreliability; no range-restriction correction because data were lacking. Structured interviews: .51 in Schmidt & Hunter (1998), corrected for both criterion unreliability and range restriction; revised to .42 by Sackett et al. (2022). Important comparability point: since neither the .54 nor the .33 work sample figure is corrected for range restriction, the drop from .54 to .33 reflects cleaner data and study selection, not a change in correction method. By contrast, much of the drop for structured interviews and GMA in Sackett et al. comes from removing what they argue were range-restriction overcorrections.
relevance_to_angle: Supports 'stop testing convergent coding' indirectly: the classic evidence base rewards realistic task samples and structured conversation over unstructured judgement, and gives no validity evidence at all for algorithm-puzzle interviews. Complicates the angle in two ways. First, the often-quoted claim that work samples are the single best predictor (.54) rests on 1984 data that Roth et al. found inflated; the better current estimate (.33) puts work samples below structured interviews (.42 in Sackett et al. 2022), which favours a structured design conversation and team-fit interview over a hands-on coding exercise. Second, Schmidt & Hunter note work samples only suit people who already know the job, which matters if 'the job' has shifted to directing agents: a pre-agent work sample may sample the wrong tasks. Supports 'design conversation' and 'communication and team fit' via the structured interview evidence; supports 'working with an agent' only if the work sample is redesigned to sample that task.
limitations_stated: Schmidt & Hunter (1998): 'This article examined the multivariate validity of only certain predictor combinations: combinations of two predictors with one of the two being GMA'; predictor combinations without GMA could not be examined because of 'the absence of the needed estimates of predictor intercorrelations'; 'some of the estimated predictor intercorrelations could not be made as precise as would be ideal'. Table note: for work samples 'The correction for range restriction was not possible in these data.' They also state work samples 'can be used only with applicants who already know the job' and have no training-performance validity data. Roth et al. (2005), per secondary course outline [uncertain on wording]: lack of information on range restriction in validity studies, which makes comparison with other predictors difficult; relatively few studies reported reliabilities; moderate number of studies compared with other predictor meta-analyses; could not report validity by exercise or dimension within work samples; only one applicant (predictive) coefficient, so no applicant vs incumbent moderator analysis.
counter_evidence: Roth et al. (2005) is itself the main counter-evidence to Schmidt & Hunter's .54: about one third lower. Sackett, Zhang, Berry & Lievens (2022, JAP; discussed in their 2023 IOP article) further argue that range-restriction corrections in prior meta-analyses were systematically overcorrected, lowering GMA from .51 to .31 and structured interviews from .51 to .42, and putting work samples at .33; they report structured interviews as the top predictor. Schmidt himself (Schmidt & Oh 2016 working paper, seen only as a search snippet) acknowledged work samples are 'somewhat less valid than had been indicated by the older data' [uncertain: not opened]. Some researchers (e.g., Ones, Viswesvaran and colleagues) have disputed Sackett et al.'s range-restriction critique [uncertain: not opened]. None of these studies involve software engineers, take-home tests or AI assistance, so extrapolating any of the figures to coding interviews is an inference, not a finding.
